selection.reason: Impact scored and summarised by Gemini.

summary: The PBM Price Transparency and Accountability Act amends titles XVIII and XIX of the Social Security Act to regulate pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) and improve pricing transparency in Medicare Part D and Medicaid. It requires transparent pass-through pricing models in Medicaid, prohibits certain forms of spread pricing, establishes pharmacy survey reporting requirements to determine actual acquisition costs, creates new accountability and reporting rules for PBMs operating in Medicare, ensures any willing pharmacy can join Medicare prescription drug plan networks under reasonable contract terms, and provides funding for government studies and oversight.

affected_groups.effect: PBMs face strict limitations on permissible fee structures (restricted to bona fide service fees), mandatory transparency and reporting requirements, prohibitions on spread pricing in Medicaid, and potential penalties or disgorgement of funds for non-compliance.

Pharmacies are required to respond to monthly acquisition cost surveys under Medicaid, gain protections regarding contract terms and network access under Medicare Part D, and are subject to civil money penalties if they fail to comply with survey reporting.

Beneficiaries may experience changes in drug coverage transparency, cost-sharing information, and pharmacy access protections as plans and PBMs adjust to new reporting, pass-through pricing, and network participation rules.
affected_groups.group: Medicaid and Medicare Part D Beneficiaries

affected_groups.effect: States must update contracts with PBMs and managed care entities to enforce pass-through pricing models, and Medicare plan sponsors must collect and submit required PBM data, oversee PBM compliance, and comply with annual certification rules.
affected_groups.group: State Medicaid Programs and Plan Sponsors

key_provisions: Establishes national average drug acquisition cost benchmarks under Medicaid via monthly surveys of retail and applicable non-retail pharmacies, backed by civil money penalties for non-compliance.

Requires state Medicaid programs to use transparent prescription drug pass-through pricing models with PBMs and managed care entities, limiting payments to ingredient cost plus fair market value professional dispensing and administrative fees while prohibiting spread pricing.

Mandates that Medicare Part D prescription drug plans permit any willing pharmacy meeting standard contract terms to participate as a network pharmacy, with standards for reasonable and relevant contract terms established by the Secretary.

Limits PBM remuneration from Medicare Part D plans and affiliates strictly to bona fide service fees (flat dollar amounts reflecting fair market value), requiring full pass-through of manufacturer rebates and discounts.

Requires PBMs under Medicare Part D to submit detailed annual reports to plan sponsors and the Secretary regarding drug utilization, pricing, dispensing channels, affiliate pricing, and manufacturer agreements.

Establishes formal processes for pharmacies to submit allegations of contract violations by Medicare Part D sponsors regarding reasonable and relevant terms, along with enforcement and audit provisions.
Appropriates specific funds for fiscal year 2026 to the HHS Inspector General, CMS Program Management Account, and MedPAC to carry out studies, oversight, and implementation.

It requires transparent pass-through pricing models in Medicaid, prohibits certain forms of spread pricing, establishes pharmacy survey reporting requirements to determine actual acquisition costs, creates new accountability and reporting rules for PBMs operating in Medicare, ensures any willing pharmacy can join Medicare prescription drug plan networks under reasonable contract terms, and provides funding for government studies and oversight.
summary_detail.significance: This bill modifies the regulatory framework governing prescription drug supply chains for federal health programs by increasing transparency on drug acquisition costs, limiting PBM compensation models, and altering contracting rules for Medicare Part D and Medicaid.
